title: RAM and ROM
starter: A computer loses power mid-lesson. Which of your work survives, and which does not? Explain why.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Why primary storage?
facts: Primary storage is memory the CPU can access directly.
Secondary storage is far too slow for the CPU to work from.
Programs and data currently in use are copied into primary storage first.
stations.challenge: Why can't the CPU just work straight from the hard drive?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Primary storage is memory the CPU can access directly.
Also credit: Secondary storage is far too slow for the CPU to work from.

questions.a: Memory the CPU can access directly, holding data and instructions in use

questions.q: Why are programs copied into RAM before they run?
questions.a: RAM is much faster than secondary storage, so the CPU doesn't have to wait

stations.name: RAM
facts: Random Access Memory: read and write, and volatile.
Holds the operating system, open applications and the data in use.
Volatile means its contents are lost when the power is switched off.
stations.challenge: List three things stored in RAM right now on the computer in front of you.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Random Access Memory: read and write, and volatile.
Also credit: Holds the operating system, open applications and the data in use.

questions.a: The contents are lost when the power is switched off

questions.q: Which is stored in RAM while a computer is running?
questions.a: The operating system and the programs currently open

stations.name: ROM
facts: Read Only Memory: read-only, and non-volatile.
Holds the boot program, often called the BIOS.
It tells the computer how to start up and load the operating system from secondary storage.
stations.challenge: Why must the start-up instructions be in ROM rather than RAM?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Read Only Memory: read-only, and non-volatile.
Also credit: Holds the boot program, often called the BIOS.

questions.a: The start-up instructions, often called the BIOS

questions.q: Why is ROM used for the boot program?
questions.a: It is non-volatile, so the instructions are still there when the power comes on

stations.name: RAM vs ROM
facts: RAM: read and write, volatile, large, holds what's in use.
ROM: read-only, non-volatile, small, holds start-up instructions.
Both are primary storage, and both are on the motherboard.
stations.challenge: Complete the RAM and ROM comparison table on your worksheet.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: RAM: read and write, volatile, large, holds what's in use.
Also credit: ROM: read-only, non-volatile, small, holds start-up instructions.

questions.q: Does each statement describe RAM or ROM?
questions.a: Volatile: loses its contents at power off = RAM; Non-volatile = ROM; Can be read from and written to = RAM; Can normally only be read from = ROM; Holds the operating system while the computer runs = RAM; Holds the BIOS or boot program = ROM

stations.name: The boot sequence
facts: Power on: the CPU runs the instructions in ROM.
The BIOS checks the hardware, then looks for the operating system.
The operating system is loaded from secondary storage into RAM, and takes over.
stations.challenge: Put the boot steps in order on your worksheet.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Power on: the CPU runs the instructions in ROM.
Also credit: The BIOS checks the hardware, then looks for the operating system.

questions.q: Put the start-up steps in order.
questions.a: The computer is switched on → The CPU runs the boot program stored in ROM → The BIOS checks the hardware is working → The operating system is copied from secondary storage into RAM → The operating system takes control

stations.name: More RAM, faster computer?
facts: If RAM fills up, the computer has to use slower secondary storage instead.
More RAM means more programs and data can be held at once.
Beyond a point, adding RAM makes little difference: the CPU or storage becomes the limit.
stations.challenge: Why does adding RAM usually make a slow computer feel faster?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: If RAM fills up, the computer has to use slower secondary storage instead.
Also credit: More RAM means more programs and data can be held at once.

questions.q: Why does a computer slow down when RAM is full?
questions.a: It has to use much slower secondary storage as extra memory

questions.q: A computer has plenty of free RAM but still feels slow. What does adding more RAM do?
questions.a: Very little: the bottleneck is somewhere else

final.name: Final challenge: primary storage

questions.q: Does each statement describe RAM, ROM, or both?
questions.a: Loses its contents when the power goes off = RAM; Holds the BIOS = ROM; Is a type of primary storage = Both; Can be written to by the operating system = RAM; Keeps its contents with no power = ROM; Is found on the motherboard = Both; Holds the programs you currently have open = RAM; Is read-only in normal use = ROM

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term volatile.
points: Random Access Memory: read and write, and volatile.
Volatile means its contents are lost when the power is switched off.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

exam.q: Describe the purpose of ROM in a computer system.
points: It tells the computer how to start up and load the operating system from secondary storage.
Holds the operating system, open applications and the data in use.
The BIOS checks the hardware, then looks for the operating system.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Explain why a computer needs primary storage.
points: Primary storage is memory the CPU can access directly.
Programs and data currently in use are copied into primary storage first.
It tells the computer how to start up and load the operating system from secondary storage.
Both are primary storage, and both are on the motherboard.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
